facts.fact_text: Shortly after the dispersal of the Erzsébet Bridge demonstration, at around 1 p.m. on 4 July 2002, more demonstrators assembled at Kossuth Square in front of the Parliament building in Budapest.
The demonstrators at Kossuth Square on 4 July 2002 demanded a recount of the April 2002 election votes.
Having learnt of the events at Kossuth Square from the news, the applicant joined the demonstration at Kossuth Square at around 7 p.m. on 4 July 2002.
Faced with an unmanageable situation, the police broke up the Kossuth Square demonstration at about 9 p.m. on 4 July 2002 without using any force.
The applicant participated in the Kossuth Square demonstration on 4 July 2002 until it was dispersed at about 9 p.m.

Article 62 of the Constitution of the Republic of Hungary (Act no. 20 of 1949 as amended) provides: "The Republic of Hungary acknowledges the right to peaceful assembly and secures its free exercise."
Faced with an unmanageable situation, the police broke up the Kossuth Square demonstration at about 9 p.m. on 4 July 2002 without using any force.
The applicant participated in the Kossuth Square demonstration on 4 July 2002 until it was dispersed at about 9 p.m.
On 1 October 2003 the Budapest Central District Court dismissed the applicant's claim.

The Budapest Central District Court found that, since the Kossuth Square demonstration had not been notified to the police as required by section 14 of the Assembly Act, the police had not had any other choice but to break it up.
The Budapest Central District Court concluded that the measures taken by the police in dispersing the Kossuth Square demonstration on 4 July 2002 had been in compliance with the law.
On 13 July 2004 the Budapest Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision of the Budapest Central District Court dismissing the applicant's claim.
The Budapest Central District Court established that the duty to inform the police about planned assemblies was applicable to every type of demonstration, including spontaneous ones.

The applicant did not deny that the Kossuth Square demonstration on 4 July 2002 had not been notified to the police, as required by section 14 of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act).

The Budapest Central District Court found that, since the Kossuth Square demonstration had not been notified to the police as required by section 14 of the Assembly Act, the police had not had any other choice but to break it up.

Section 6 of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act) provides that the organisation of an event held in the public domain shall be notified to the competent police headquarters according to the place of the event, and in Budapest to the Budapest Police Headquarters, three days prior to the planned date of the event, and that the obligation to notify the police lies with the organiser of the event.

Section 14(1) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the relevant time, provides that the police shall disperse an event if the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly contravenes section 2(3) of the Assembly Act, or if the participants appear at the event in possession of arms, or if an event subject to prior notification is held without notification, or despite a decision banning the event.

By the time the applicant joined the demonstration at Kossuth Square at around 7 p.m. on 4 July 2002, traffic and public transport — including the circulation of trams and trolley-buses — had become seriously disrupted in the area of Kossuth Square.
The police eventually had to close some streets nearby Kossuth Square during the demonstration on 4 July 2002.

The Budapest Central District Court found that the duty to inform the police in advance about assemblies held in public served the protection of the public interest and the rights of others, namely the prevention of disorder and the undisturbed circulation of traffic.

Section 2(3) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act) provides that the exercise of freedom of assembly shall not constitute a crime or an incitement to crime, and moreover, it should not result in the infringement of the rights and freedoms of others.

Section 8(1) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the relevant time, provides that if the holding of an event subject to prior notification seriously endangers the proper functioning of the representative bodies or courts, or results in a disproportionate hindrance of the circulation of traffic, the police may ban the holding of the event at the place or time indicated in the notification, within 48 hours from the receipt of the notification by the authority.

On the morning of Thursday, 4 July 2002, several hundred demonstrators started to protest against the statutory destruction of the ballots from the April 2002 elections, which was scheduled for 20 to 22 July 2002.
The demonstrators who blocked Erzsébet Bridge on 4 July 2002 had not given prior notice of their gathering to the police, as required by Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act).
The demonstrators who assembled at Kossuth Square at around 1 p.m. on 4 July 2002 did so without any prior notification to the police.

By the time the applicant joined the demonstration at Kossuth Square at around 7 p.m. on 4 July 2002, traffic and public transport — including the circulation of trams and trolley-buses — had become seriously disrupted in the area of Kossuth Square.
The police initially attempted to allow the circulation of traffic to continue during the Kossuth Square demonstration on 4 July 2002.
Faced with an unmanageable situation, the police broke up the Kossuth Square demonstration at about 9 p.m. on 4 July 2002 without using any force.

The Budapest Central District Court found that, since the Kossuth Square demonstration had not been notified to the police as required by section 14 of the Assembly Act, the police had not had any other choice but to break it up.

Section 14(1) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the relevant time, provides that the police shall disperse an event if the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly contravenes section 2(3) of the Assembly Act, or if the participants appear at the event in possession of arms, or if an event subject to prior notification is held without notification, or despite a decision banning the event.
